Why it is here: In-depth reporting, original content, and clear, well-structured English.

When John Nelson died in the summer of 2025, he left behind more than 400 explosive devices, a literal minefield that ran through his home in the suburbs between Manchester and Liverpool. The painstaking work of clearing Nelson’s home of explosives prompted “one of the largest domestic evacuations of its kind in recent British history,” writes Andrew Kersley, who spent months interviewing the experts who kept Nelson’s home from exploding, as well as the neighbors who seemingly loved him. “I guess it was just his pastime,” one tells Kersley. Indeed!

During a second search after Nelson’s death, police had discovered a small tobacco tin containing explosives, with wires protruding from it. RY set up his X-ray machine and stepped into the adjoining room while it scanned the tin. As he reached for the door, he almost triggered the first booby trap: a fishing line wrapped around the handle that was attached to a rigged shotgun cartridge. Suddenly the contents of the house looked rather different. If one door had been trapped, any of them might be. So might any of the shoulder-high piles surrounding him.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Thoughtful exploration of a topic with a focus on learning and originality.

Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

Whenever I clean spinach or other greens, I get a curious feeling. I see a post-apocalyptic future, where a white-haired version of me is cleaning greens amid the ruins, salvaging every tiny, edible leaf. I then imagine my ancestors doing the same thing a hundred thousand years ago. Nothing heroic about this work, no high drama, no awesome mammoth-hunting. Just the fundamental stuff that keeps life going.

“In the temperate and tropical regions where it appears that hominids evolved into human beings, the principal food of the species was vegetable,” Ursula K. Le Guin reminds us in her classic The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction. “Sixty-five to eighty percent of what human beings ate in those regions in Paleolithic, Neolithic, and prehistoric times was gathered; only in the extreme Arctic was meat the staple food.”

Vegetables have quietly sustained us, season after season, year after year, for millennia. Down-to-earth and seemingly mundane, they claim deep love and reverence from those who care to look. Over time, we have even come to imbue vegetables with drama, heroes, stories. Are they (and we) made better by the act? Or do they only require simple, loving attention?

When Edward Espe Brown, Zen monk and chef, was a young student at the Tassajara Zen Mountain Center in California, he asked his teacher, Shunryū Suzuki Rōshi, for advice on working in the kitchen. “When you wash the rice,” Rōshi told him, “wash the rice. When you cut the carrots, cut the carrots. When you stir the soup, stir the soup.”

It takes a long time to understand vegetables, cooking, and giving and receiving nourishing food. But what if that is only one half of the truth, one way of looking at things? What if it also takes no time at all, and we can understand everything right this moment? “Appreciate this carrot, cabbage, cucumber, and cress, this time with the less than perfect,” Brown reminds us. “The remarkable flavor you have searched for is everywhere. Let it come home to your heart.” Bon appétit!

Can Babies Learn to Love Vegetables? (Burkhard Bilger, The New Yorker, November 2019)

Every Halloween, Linus sits in the “most sincere” pumpkin patch with a signboard, awaiting the arrival of The Great Pumpkin. Will he come this year? Watch the 1966 classic “It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown” on Apple TV.

I’ve always been a vegetarian. You might think that would make me biased toward vegetables, and you’d be right. But when I was little, I routinely fantasized about installing a zipper in my belly so I could just shove the little devils in without ever taking my eyes off my comics. I eventually grew to love them, but could something have been done to smooth the way earlier?

The title question must be asked, for that’s where the story begins—babies and their smushed-up veggies. Bilger seeks an answer.

The enemy in question is kale. The four cups are all filled with raw kale leaves whipped into a smooth purée, or slurry, as food researchers call it. One sample is plain, another sweet, another sweeter still, and the last one salted. Sugar and salt can mask the bitterness in kale, but this baby isn’t fooled. No matter which sample he’s offered, he grimaces and turns his head, purses his lips, and swats the spoon away. The more his mother tries, the grumpier he gets, till he kicks his foot so hard that he jostles the electrode, disrupting the signal.

Stalking the Vegetannual (Barbara Kingsolver, Orion, March/April 2007)

Way before the Potato of Immaculate Conception, in the Middle Ages, there was the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary—“a strange hybrid creature, half-animal, half-plant.” Thom Sliwowski investigates old vegetable fancies for The Public Domain Review in “Animal, Vegetable, Lamb: The Zoophyte from Tartary.”

“Wait a minute,” a friend asks Kingsolver, “When you say, ‘the potatoes are up,’ what do you mean?” An urban, gourmet chef, she tries to puzzle it out some more: “What part of a potato comes up?” I find it somewhat hard to believe that a chef might not know the potato has a plant part, but who knows with us modern humans? We buy the vegetables that look appealing (and feel affordable) at the shop, never mind the season or the provenance.

Kingsolver has a remedy. She gives us “a roadmap to eating with the seasons”—a beautiful visual mnemonic, if you will, one you’re unlikely to forget once you’ve successfully pictured it. What’s better, it’s actually useful.

To recover an intuitive sense of what will be in season throughout the year, picture an imaginary plant that bears over the course of one growing season all the different vegetable products we can harvest. We’ll call it a vegetannual. Picture its life passing before your eyes like a time-lapse film: first, in the cool early spring, shoots poke up out of the ground. Small leaves appear, then bigger leaves. As the plant grows up into the sunshine and the days grow longer, flower buds will appear, followed by small green fruits. Under midsummer’s warm sun, the fruits grow larger, riper, and more colorful. As days shorten into the autumn, these mature into hard-shelled fruits with appreciable seeds inside. Finally, as the days grow cool, the vegetannual may hoard the sugars its leaves have made, pulling them down into a storage unit of some kind: a tuber, bulb, or root.…

Why it is here: Engaging and informative, with a focus on a specific event and its context.

Black and tan coonhound Rocker is top dog at the 2026 National Dog Show

An enthusiastic black and tan coonhound with a glossy coat and big floppy ears named Rocker is top dog at this year's National Dog Show — the most widely viewed dog competition in the country.

Rocker took the prestigious best in show prize after defeating six other dogs who each won top honors in their groups. Rocker earned first place among the hound group.

Best in show judge Lorraine Bisso commended Rocker's looks and physical agility.

"He's got a very masculine head. It's correct for the breed in terms of length and width," Bisso said. "He has beautiful feet. He has a lovely forechest — which is necessary, because he's going to run for 25 miles. I mean, this is a hunting hound."

Bisso extended her praise to Rocker's handler, Mandy Clevenger, who has handled the coonhound since he started his career as a show dog as a pup.

"The mark of a good handler is to fade into the background and let the dog speak for itself," Bisso said.

Judges assess the competitors based on the codified ideals of their respective breeds, judging them on physical structure and temperamental characteristics. Around 2,000 canines compete each year for honors like best of breed, first in group, and the top best in show title.

"I just didn't expect it," said Clevenger of the win, adding that Rocker appeared to enjoy himself throughout the competition. "He loves the crowd," Clevenger said.

Rocker, who is owned by Traci Mitchell of Bedford, Iowa, is used to earning top honors. Thursday's title was Rocker's 15th best in show. The coonhound is expected to compete at the Westminster Kennel Club Dog Show early next year in New York City.

Victors in the other six groups for 2026 include a lhasa apso named Kissy in the non-sporting group; Biggie Smalls, a Newfoundland in the working category; and, in the terrier contest, a Norfolk terrier named Rambo.

NBC broadcast the annual event on Thanksgiving, as the network has done since 2002. It was also streamed on Peacock. Former Seinfeld star John O'Hurley, sports commentator Mary Carillo, and canine expert David Frei hosted the show, which was held in person at the Greater Philadelphia Expo Center on Nov. 14 and 15.

Last year's best in show winner was Soleil, a Belgian sheepdog.

The Kennel Club of Philadelphia originally launched its dog show in 1879 – and has organized it annually since 1933 – long before the televised National Dog Show era began in 2002 with NBC's partnership with the club and sponsor Purina.

Owing to the rescheduled Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, NBC plans to rebroadcast the National Dog Show on Saturday from noon to 2 p.m., following the rescheduled parade.

item.title: Nothing but Highlights: Is Power Slap the Sport We Deserve?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Interesting topic but lacks depth and originality, more of a sports feature than a cultural or educational piece.

Slapping someone in the face is now a sport. Yes, I’m surprised too. But in an era of ever-shrinking attention spans, getting to the point (or the slap) within seconds seems to be the surest way to hold viewers. According to its founder, Dana White, “Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade.” Stuart McGurk deftly guides us through the rise of the slap, and talks with those who fear the consequences of hitting someone round the head as hard as you can.

The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.
